WITH handover AS (
  SELECT nullif($1::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS item
),
claim AS (
  SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN h.item ->> 'run_id' ~ '^[0-9]{1,18}$'
      THEN (h.item ->> 'run_id')::bigint
    END AS run_id
  FROM handover h
),
run AS (
  SELECT r.domain_id
  FROM runs r
  WHERE r.id = (SELECT run_id FROM claim)
)
-- The first node after the trigger, and the shape the parent design fixes for every
-- workflow in this set (.specs/2026-08-19-research-pipeline-port.md, section 4): the
-- domain's personas and taxonomy, read as ONE query answering exactly one row. Both
-- halves are argued in full on ar-ingest's Load Domain Context, which asks the same
-- question of the same tables and is not repeated here. What is written out below is
-- the half that differs, which is how this canvas gets a domain at all.

-- It gets one off a RUN, and off no member of the hand-over item. The caller opened
-- nothing: the runs row this reads is the one ar-dispatch opened for the claimed
-- topic and ar-ingest is accounting for, and its id is what travels. A domain named
-- on the item as well would be a second statement of something that row already
-- carries, and two statements of one fact can disagree with nothing reporting it.
-- What a research pass records is charged to a run, so the domain it is filed under
-- is the run's.

-- The whole hand-over item binds as ONE jsonb parameter rather than one parameter per
-- member. An item reaching this trigger by hand may be anything at all,
-- JSON.stringify makes every one of those a valid jsonb literal, and the members are
-- then read where a comment can say what each one is instead of inside an expression
-- no gate reads. The nullif is the other half of that: JSON.stringify(null) binds the
-- JSON null literal rather than SQL NULL, so an invocation carrying no item at all
-- would otherwise arrive here as a value.

-- ->> answers NULL for every jsonb that is not an object, so an item that is not one
-- needs no guard in front of the read: the pattern test is handed NULL, the CASE
-- answers NULL, and nothing raises over a shape somebody else chose. It renders a
-- number as text as readily as a string, which is what lets one read cover both
-- spellings an id can arrive in.

-- The digit bound is {1,18} rather than +, and the difference between them is a
-- raise. A longer run of digits matches + and then overflows the bigint cast, which
-- is an error this node could not survive: eighteen digits sits inside bigint's
-- nineteen, and no runs id is going to reach it.

-- Three readings come out of this row and they are not two. A null run_id means the
-- item named no run this statement could read. A run_id with a null domain_id means
-- it named one that matches no runs row. A domain row means the pass resolved, and
-- an empty list beside it is a domain that states no personas, no categories, no
-- terms or no criteria. Read them in that order: a length says nothing until both
-- have been read.

-- Nothing here refuses. Every intention this pass is asked to drain is a row
-- somebody else already raised and an operator already ruled on, so a refusal at the
-- top of this workflow leaves those rows unstamped with nothing recording why. What
-- this answers instead is a row saying what it could and could not resolve.

-- run_id travels as the parameter rather than as a column read back, so it survives
-- a run id that resolves to nothing. It has to travel because this node's answer
-- REPLACES the item the trigger was handed: the rest of the hand-over is the claimed
-- topic, its id and the two interval bounds a proposed gap is clamped against, and
-- whatever node below needs those reaches all of it at
-- $('Execute Workflow Trigger').first().json, which is the handle every node here
-- has on the invocation. Reading that is the proposing group's rather than this
-- node's.

-- Every list is ordered, which nothing downstream requires and every reader benefits
-- from: two passes over one unchanged domain hand the nodes below the same lists in
-- the same order, so a diff between two runs is about the candidates rather than
-- about the order a planner happened to return rows in.
SELECT
  (SELECT run_id FROM claim) AS run_id,
  (SELECT domain_id FROM run) AS domain_id,
  -- The domain row, cut to the members a research pass reads, and shorter than the
  -- one ar-ingest and ar-score fetch. Those two carry feature_version and
  -- embedding_model because a feature vector is composed on those canvases, and
  -- nothing here composes one: a projection copied whole would be two columns
  -- travelling to no reader, and a reader added later would be reading a pin nobody
  -- here maintains. What is left is the identity an operator reads a pass by and the
  -- settings a display vocabulary comes out of. NULL rather than an empty object
  -- when the item named no run this statement could resolve, which is the second of
  -- the three readings above.
  (SELECT jsonb_build_object(
     'id', d.id,
     'slug', d.slug,
     'name', d.name,
     'settings', d.settings)
     FROM domains d
    WHERE d.id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)) AS domain,

  -- The personas. system_text is operator-owned prose and is the trusted half of
  -- what prompt-frame.ts composes around an untrusted chunk, and the whole list
  -- travels rather than the one row a step needs: which role a step is framed
  -- against is that step's to decide, and picking a row out of a list already here
  -- is a read rather than a second query per role. A persona is a row and is never
  -- written into a file, and no node below may put a candidate's own text where one
  -- belongs.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', p.id,
       'role', p.role,
       'system_text', p.system_text)
       ORDER BY p.role, p.id)
       FROM personas p
      WHERE p.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS personas,

  -- The categories, which are the buckets the terms below are filed under. key
  -- rather than id is what a reader downstream matches on: a library reading a
  -- category reads its key, so the surrogate id travels for an operator's benefit
  -- and the key is what the code matches.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', c.id,
       'key', c.key,
       'name', c.name,
       'parent_id', c.parent_id)
       ORDER BY c.key, c.id)
       FROM categories c
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS categories,

  -- The terms, joined to their category's key rather than carrying category_id.
  -- Four members and this exact spelling, because the libraries reading this one
  -- list each read a different subset of it: feature-version.ts takes all four,
  -- features.ts takes pattern and category, and static-gate.ts takes pattern, weight
  -- and polarity. A term list selected without the join satisfies one reader and
  -- starves the others, with nothing failing.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'category', c.key,
       'pattern', t.pattern,
       'weight', t.weight,
       'polarity', t.polarity)
       ORDER BY c.key, t.pattern, t.id)
       FROM terms t
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = t.category_id
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS terms,

  -- The criteria, joined to their category the same way. Nothing in a research pass
  -- scores anything: criteria are ar-score's subject, and a pass here is about what
  -- is known of one candidate rather than about how a finding measures up against a
  -- position the domain stated. They are selected because the design fixes the
  -- taxonomy as what this node fetches, and the taxonomy is these three tables, so a
  -- node group added below reads them without a second lookup and without a second
  -- branch to reason about.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', k.id,
       'category', c.key,
       'value', k.value,
       'kind', k.kind)
       ORDER BY c.key, k.kind, k.id)
       FROM criteria k
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = k.category_id
      WHERE k.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS criteria

-- Where an approved intention becomes work, and the first node on this canvas that
-- decides what the pass is about. The node above resolved a domain; this one reads
-- the rulings a person has already made against it, and hands the groups below one
-- item per candidate to research.

-- NOTHING HERE APPROVES ANYTHING. research_pool in src/db/schema/entities.ts is the
-- gate, and what fills it happens elsewhere entirely: an intention is raised by
-- ar-ingest or by ar-score, and approved_at is written by a person through
-- scripts/approve.ts and, after that, through the API and the UI. This statement
-- reads the result of those rulings and makes none of its own. No node on this canvas
-- writes approved_at, and no branch here stands in for one.

-- A PENDING ROW IS INVISIBLE TO THIS QUERY, which is what the gate buys at the drain.
-- It is not selected, not counted, and not named by the group that closes this pass,
-- so a domain whose queue nobody has worked through drains nothing and spends
-- nothing. That is the outcome rather than a gap: an intention nobody consented to is
-- exactly what this pipeline must not act on, and never seeing one is the cheapest
-- way of not acting on it.

-- STATUS AND THE TIMESTAMPS ARE TWO ACCOUNTS OF ONE ROW, and this statement reads
-- only the first. research_pool.status records where a row stands and nothing refuses
-- a writer that sets any member at any time, while research_pool_approval_check at
-- the foot of that table reads approved_at and researched_at alone. So a row stamped
-- approved whose approved_at is still NULL is storable, and it is selected here.

-- What refuses it is the database, at the write, and that is the design rather than
-- an oversight. The record group below inserts the entity_research row and stamps
-- researched_at in ONE statement, so a subject nobody approved takes neither half. A
-- branch here would not be the same thing: a branch governs the writes one workflow
-- issues and leaves every other writer to its own habits, which is the argument that
-- table makes in full.

-- What that costs is worth naming rather than implying. A row in that state reaches
-- the model call before the write refuses it, so the call is billed and nothing is
-- recorded, and the row stays open and comes round again. It is a misconfiguration
-- somebody has to fix, and a run reporting a refused write is how they find out.

-- OLDEST FIRST, so a queue worked top-down empties rather than churns. The row at
-- risk of never being drained is the one that has waited longest, and a newest-first
-- pass pushes it further down every time an intention is raised. listPending in
-- scripts/approve.ts orders the review queue the same way and for the same reason, so
-- the operator reading the queue and the pass draining it agree about which end
-- matters.

-- created_at does not order these rows on its own. now() is the transaction's start
-- time, so every intention one pass raised carries the same value to the microsecond
-- and timestamptz stores nothing finer. id breaks the tie, which is what makes two
-- passes over one unchanged queue take the same batch rather than merely look stable.

-- A BOUNDED BATCH, and the bound is a spending ceiling rather than paging.
-- research_pool says what it is for: a queue nobody is watching must not turn into a
-- single expensive run, so a hundred approved rows are researched over many passes.
-- Twenty five is the number the rest of this set bounds a batch with, both
-- AR_DISPATCH_BATCH_CAP in scripts/workflow-markers.ts and ar-ingest's
-- MAX_MODEL_CALLS_PER_RUN holding it, and it is written out here because a statement
-- can splice nothing and no marker declares it. Moving it to ENV_DEFAULTS is that
-- edit plus its own entry in that table rather than something to imply here.

-- IT IS NOT THE CALL CEILING. This bounds the rows the pass CARRIES: the projection
-- below reads documents for every one of them, and the gate above the model group
-- runs every one of them through a validator. What the pass may SPEND is declared
-- again in that group, over what survives the gate, which is never more rows than
-- this and is usually fewer. The two bound different things and coincide in value,
-- and neither is derived from the other.

-- A ROW PAST THE BOUND IS NOT DROPPED. It keeps its approval and its open stamp, so
-- the next pass finds it at the head of this same order. That is unlike the cap in
-- ar-dispatch, which drops rows already claimed and rescheduled and leaves them a
-- whole interval, and unlike the ceiling in ar-ingest, where a document left outside
-- the bound is never offered again at all.

-- A ROW THAT CANNOT BE RESEARCHED IS THE COST OF OLDEST FIRST, and settling it
-- belongs to the groups below. Nothing stamped stays at the head, so an intention the
-- record group refuses is fetched first again by the next pass and paid for again.
-- research_pool.researched_at is where that is argued and where the answer is stated:
-- a row the drain cannot act on is closed with its reason kept rather than left open,
-- which is the failure the design this port draws from met and fixed.

-- ONE ITEM PER CANDIDATE. A Postgres node maps its statement over the items it was
-- handed and passes on what the statement returned, and Load Domain Context above
-- answers exactly one row, so this node runs once and answers as many items as it
-- drained. Every group below is one item's work: the gate validates one name, the
-- framing node prepares one chunk, and the record group writes one result.

-- Which also means this node's answer REPLACES the context item, the way that item
-- replaced the one the trigger was handed. The personas, the categories and the terms
-- are not gone: a node below reaches them at $('Load Domain Context').first().json,
-- and the claimed topic a proposed gap is clamped against is still at
-- $('Execute Workflow Trigger').first().json.

-- AN EMPTY DRAIN EMITS NO ITEM, and a node handed no item does not run, so a pass
-- with nothing approved ends here rather than below. That is the ordinary state of
-- most passes, intentions being raised on every ingest and ruled on when somebody has
-- time. What a pass that drained nothing records is the canvas topology's to answer
-- rather than this statement's.

-- TWO PARAMETERS, in declaration order: the run and the domain. Both are read off the
-- context item above rather than out of the hand over a second time. That node has
-- already resolved the domain off the run, and deriving it a second way here is how
-- the two start being able to disagree. A NULL domain selects nothing, which is where
-- a pass started by hand ends.

SELECT
-- WHAT TRAVELS IS CUT TO WHAT THE GROUPS BELOW READ, on the rule Load Domain Context
-- above applies to its own projection: a column travelling to no reader is a column a
-- reader added later starts maintaining without knowing it. So created_at and
-- approved_at order this batch and do not travel, and finding_id is read by the
-- documents subquery below and travels no further than that.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,

  -- The intention itself, and the only handle on it that survives the item
  -- replacement above. The record group addresses this row by id when it stamps
  -- researched_at, and nothing below re-derives which intention it is working on: a
  -- second derivation of that is how a result comes to close a row it did not come
  -- from. domain_id travels beside it so an item says which domain it belongs to
  -- without reaching back for the context, and the predicate below is what makes it
  -- the parameter's.
  p.id AS pool_id,
  p.domain_id,

  -- The exact strings an operator approved, carried rather than composed.
  -- research_pool.search_terms is the gate's substance: the approval was given to
  -- these and not to a description of what would be assembled later, so a node below
  -- that built its own would be issuing something nobody ruled on. An empty list is a
  -- real state and means an intention nobody could turn into a query, which is a row
  -- the groups below close rather than search for nothing.
  p.search_terms,

  -- The subject, resolved one hop through alias_of, and NOT the column the pool row
  -- carries. entities.alias_of states the reader's rule, COALESCE(alias_of, id), and
  -- why a merge is a pointer rather than a rewrite: a placeholder keeps its own row
  -- and its own history and readers resolve through it. So an intention raised
  -- against a placeholder is researched as the subject it turned out to be, and the
  -- entity_research row is filed under that subject rather than under the row that
  -- stood in for it. This is the id that column takes.
  --
  -- One hop and no further, which is that column's rule as well: a chain resolves to
  -- whatever its first hop names and a self-alias resolves to the row itself, so
  -- neither loops a reader here any more than anywhere else.
  --
  -- NULL where the intention names no subject at all, which research_pool.entity_id
  -- calls an ordinary state rather than a gap: an intention can be raised from a
  -- finding whose subject nothing has attributed, and the terms above are what make
  -- it researchable anyway. What a pass may ask about a candidate carrying no name is
  -- the gate below's to decide rather than this statement's.
  e.id AS entity_id,
  e.name AS entity_name,

  -- The documents behind the candidate, and the whole of the material this pass is
  -- asked to research it against. Every one of them is a row this domain already
  -- captured: nothing here reaches outside the corpus, and what a model is later
  -- handed is a chunk prepared from these bodies rather than anything fetched.
  --
  -- WHICH DOCUMENTS. The finding that raised the intention is always one of them,
  -- because it is the occasion an operator approved and a bound able to cut it would
  -- offer a model everything except the reason the row exists. The rest are the
  -- documents of the other findings attributed to the same subject, which is what
  -- makes this a candidate's corpus rather than one document's.
  --
  -- The subject test reads both spellings, the id the intention named and the id it
  -- resolved to, so a placeholder's own findings and its target's are both here. What
  -- it does not reach is a THIRD row aliased to the same subject: that would be a
  -- resolution per finding rather than one join, and its findings are simply not
  -- offered. Saying so is the point rather than fixing it here.
  --
  -- BOUNDED AT FIVE PER CANDIDATE, which is what keeps this projection from carrying
  -- a subject's whole history. Bodies travel whole, this node answering one item per
  -- drained row, so what a pass carries is five documents times the batch bound
  -- below. The occasioning document is ordered first so the bound can never drop it,
  -- and newest first after that, on the reading ar-ingest's own corpus window takes:
  -- recent material is what a reader wants, and the id is what makes recent
  -- deterministic.
  --
  -- The set and the order are two different jobs, which is why there are two ORDER
  -- BYs. The inner one decides WHICH five and reads the aggregate, the outer one
  -- emits them ascending by id, so two passes over one unchanged corpus hand the
  -- groups below the same list in the same order.
  --
  -- GROUP BY d.id alone, the primary key functionally determining the other three
  -- members, which is what lets one document carrying several of the subject's
  -- findings arrive once rather than once per finding.
  --
  -- Four members each. id is what a citation names, and researchBriefErrors in
  -- src/lib/research-brief.ts judges an answer's citations against exactly the ids
  -- offered here, so this list IS the offered set. url is provenance for a person
  -- reading a result. body is what a chunk is built from. parse_status travels beside
  -- it because a document whose parse failed still has a row and may still have an
  -- empty body, and the group preparing a chunk has to be able to say which of the
  -- two it is looking at.
  --
  -- An empty list is a real answer rather than a failure: an intention naming no
  -- subject and no finding has nothing behind it, and it is the terms above that were
  -- approved in that case.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', b.id,
       'url', b.url,
       'parse_status', b.parse_status,
       'body', b.body)
       ORDER BY b.id)
       FROM (
         SELECT d.id, d.url, d.parse_status, d.body
           FROM findings f
           JOIN documents d ON d.id = f.document_id
          WHERE f.domain_id = p.domain_id
            AND (f.id = p.finding_id
                 OR (p.entity_id IS NOT NULL
                     AND f.entity_id IN (p.entity_id, e.id)))
          GROUP BY d.id
          ORDER BY bool_or(f.id = p.finding_id) DESC NULLS LAST, d.id DESC
          LIMIT 5) b),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS documents

-- The pool row, and the two joins that name its subject. The first reads the entity
-- the intention named and the second reads the one that names resolves to, both LEFT
-- because research_pool.entity_id is nullable and an intention naming no subject is
-- an ordinary row rather than one to drop. Neither join can fail to find its target
-- where there is one: alias_of carries ON DELETE no action, so an entity an alias
-- points at cannot be deleted out from under it.
FROM research_pool p
LEFT JOIN entities n ON n.id = p.entity_id
LEFT JOIN entities e ON e.id = COALESCE(n.alias_of, n.id)

-- The predicate, three rules and none standing in for another. domain_id keeps the
-- pass inside the domain its run was opened for, and researching another domain's
-- approved intention would be work nobody in this pass consented to. status is the
-- ruling. researched_at IS NULL is the row still being open, which is the second half
-- of what that column reserves: closed rather than researched, so a row the drain
-- closed without a search is out of this set too and does not come round again.
WHERE p.domain_id = $2::bigint
  AND p.status = 'approved'
  AND p.researched_at IS NULL
ORDER BY p.created_at, p.id
LIMIT 25

parameters.content:
## One Caller, No Clock

This workflow is invoked, and by `ar-ingest` rather than by the dispatcher. A pull pass reaches it through an Execute Workflow node once it has written and scored what it found, and the Execute Workflow Trigger on this canvas is the whole of what makes that possible.

`ar-dispatch` does not invoke it, and could not be made to without a table that does not exist. The only two schedulable tables are `topics` and `export_subscriptions`, and a research unit is neither of them. A pass here also needs a claimed topic in hand: the gap it may propose is clamped against that topic's own `min_interval_seconds` and `max_interval_seconds`, and the topic is what the dispatcher already claimed and handed on. So the invocation sits where the topic still is.

It holds no clock and may not acquire one: `ar-dispatch` carries the only Schedule Trigger in the system, and `tests/invariants/workflows.test.ts` counts them across every built workflow and names the one file allowed to hold one. The Execute Workflow Trigger here registers nothing when a workflow is activated, so `scripts/activate-workflows.sh` reports this file manual-only and leaves it inactive. That is the outcome rather than a gap: what starts this workflow is a caller, and a caller needs no registration.

### What arrives

One item. `run_id` is the run the calling pass is accounting for, which is the row `ar-dispatch` opened for the claimed topic rather than one this workflow or its caller opened. The claim travels beside it: the topic's id and its two interval bounds, which are what a proposed gap is later clamped against.

`Load Domain Context` reads the first of those and no more, and reads the domain back off the run rather than off a member of the item. The rest stays where it arrived, reachable at `$('Execute Workflow Trigger').first().json`, because this node's answer REPLACES the item the trigger was handed. Which node reads the claim is the group that proposes a gap, and reading it is that group's rather than this node's.

The trigger is typeVersion 1, which passes the caller's item through as it stands. Nothing here declares an input schema, so what the caller sends is what the first node reads, and adding a schema later is a change to both ends rather than to this node alone.

### Started by hand

A run started from this canvas rather than by a caller carries no `run_id`, and nothing pretends otherwise. `Load Domain Context` answers a null `run_id`, a null `domain_id`, a null domain row and four empty lists, which is a shape a node below can refuse by name. It is not an error worth suppressing: a pass with no run to charge has nowhere to write what it did, and a pass with no domain has no approved intention to drain, so it drains nothing rather than researching a candidate nobody asked about.

## A Ruling Becomes Work

`Drain Approved Intentions` is where a person's decision stops being a row in a queue and starts costing something. Everything above it is about a domain. Everything below it is about the candidates somebody said yes to.

`research_pool` in `src/db/schema/entities.ts` is the gate, and its whole argument is that noticing a subject is worth looking into and actually looking are separate events, written by different things at different times. `ar-ingest` and `ar-score` do the noticing, one intention per finding. A person does the ruling, through `scripts/approve.ts` today and through the API and the UI after that. This canvas does the looking, and only for what was ruled on.

### A pending row is invisible to this query

The drain selects on a `status` of `approved` and a `researched_at` that is still NULL. A row nobody has looked at holds the `pending` default, fails the first of those, and is not selected, not counted, and not named by the group that closes the pass.

That is the outcome rather than a gap. A queue nobody has worked through drains nothing and spends nothing, so a run over a domain whose intentions are all pending researched no one and cost nothing. Read such a run as a queue waiting on a person, not as a pipeline that found nothing to do.

### Nothing on this canvas approves anything

No node here writes `approved_at`, and no branch here stands in for one. A workflow able to approve its own intentions would be a second gate beside the one an operator uses, and it would sit where nobody reviews it: the instance is a deploy target rather than a source, so a guard changed on a canvas is lost at the next import and reaches no diff on the way.

What refuses a row nobody approved is the database. `research_pool_approval_check` reads `approved_at` and `researched_at` and refuses any row recording that it was closed without recording that it was approved first. The record group below stamps `researched_at` in the SAME statement that inserts the `entity_research` row, so an unapproved subject takes neither half.

That check is the gate rather than a backstop behind one, and the drain does not duplicate it. `status` and the two timestamps are separate accounts of one row: nothing refuses a writer that sets `status` to `approved` without writing `approved_at`, so a row in that state IS drained here, does reach the model call, and is refused at the write. The call is billed and nothing is recorded. It is a misconfiguration somebody has to fix, and a run reporting a refused write is how they find out about it.

### What the drain decides, and what it does not

It does not decide who is researched: that is the ruling, and it was made before this pass started. It does not decide what is asked: the strings are `research_pool.search_terms`, stored when the intention was raised so an operator reads the exact terms before they are sent rather than an account of what would be assembled later. It does not decide whether a candidate may be asked about at all: every drained name goes through `validateEntityName` in the gate below first.

What it decides is how many and in what order. Oldest first, so a queue worked top-down empties rather than churns and the row that has waited longest is the one taken. Bounded, so a queue nobody is watching cannot become one expensive run, a hundred approved rows being researched over many passes rather than all at once. A row past the bound is not dropped: it keeps its approval and its open stamp, and it is at the head of the next pass.
